ESE 3105 Study Pack

Heat and Mass Transfer. One-shot notes, then every shortlisted past-paper topic (2019-2023) with full answers, slide figures and worked numericals. Your place, theme and text size are remembered on this device.

24-hour priority list

You answer 3 of 4 questions in each part, so each part has its own list. Study down both lists until the green pass line: about 3 h for Part A and 4 h for Part B, which leaves time for sleep and a last read of the one-shot notes. Alternate between parts (A block 1, B block 1, A block 2 …) so neither is left short. Chance: how often the topic came up, newer papers weigh more (2023 ×5, 2022 ×4, 2021 ×3, 2020 ×2, 2019 ×1). Covered: share of that part's past-paper marks you have studied once you finish the row.

Retake tip: read the Concept Primer first (30 minutes). In Part A the wall/pipe resistance numerical (A2), critical radius (A3) and the fin derivation plus numerical (A4) come every year and all have calculators. The boiling curve (A6) is pure theory: learn the five regions. In Part B learn the dimensionless numbers (B1) and the flat-plate numerical (B3); natural convection on a plate (B6) is the easiest numerical. Tube banks (B5) are long: do them last.

One-shot notes: ESE 3105 Heat and Mass Transfer

Modes and conduction equation (A1)

Conduction Q = −kA dT/dx (Fourier); convection Q = hA(Ts − T∞) (Newton); radiation Q = εσA(Ts4 − Tsur4), σ = 5.67×10−8. α = k/ρcp (how fast heat spreads).

Cartesian: ∂/∂x(k∂T/∂x) + ... + ė = ρc ∂T/∂t. Cylinder: (1/r)∂/∂r(kr∂T/∂r) + (1/r2)∂/∂φ(k∂T/∂φ) + ∂/∂z(k∂T/∂z) + ė = ρc∂T/∂t. Laplace/Poisson/diffusion forms.

BCs: temperature, flux, insulated, convection, radiation, interface. Generation = conversion, not creation. Contact resistance Rc = ΔT/(Q/A): roughness, pressure, hardness, fluid in gaps.

Resistances (A2)

Wall L/kA; film 1/hA; cylinder ln(r2/r1)/2πkL; sphere (r2 − r1)/4πkr1r2; Q = ΔT/ΣR; 1/U = 1/h1 + L/k + 1/h2.

Wire with ė: T0 − Ts = ėr02/4k, Q = ėπr02L. k = k0(1 + βt) ⇒ km at mean temperature.

Answers: wall 85 °C/6300 W; wall + film 7.39 kW; brick 518 W; steam pipe 121 W/m, ΔTins 284 °C; wire 149.4/152.7 °C.

Critical radius (A3)

R = ln(r2/r1)/2πkL + 1/2πr2hL; dR/dr2 = 0 ⇒ rcr = k/h (cylinder), 2k/h (sphere). Q is max at rcr. Below rcr insulation increases loss (good for electric wires); removing sub-critical insulation reduces loss.

Fins (A4)

d2θ/dx2 − m2θ = 0, m = √(hp/kAc) (pin √(4h/kD)). Insulated tip: θ/θb = cosh m(L − x)/cosh mL, Q = √(hpkAc)θbtanh mL. Long: tanh = 1. Corrected Lc = L + Ac/p.

η = tanh mL/mL; ε = Qfin/hAbθb (> 2 to be worth it). Longer: more effective, less efficient. Rod 25.1 W; parabolic pin η 0.985, 1.82 W; motor: bare 356 W ≥ 350 W (no fins needed: flag).

Transient (A5)

Bi = hLc/k, Lc = V/A (sphere D/6, cylinder D/4, plate L/2); Bi < 0.1 ⇒ lumped. θ/θi = e−bt, b = hA/ρVcp, bt = Bi·Fo.

One-term: θ0 = A1e−λ12τ (Bi = hr0/k); Q/Qmax = 1 − 2θ0J1(λ1)/λ1. Semi-infinite: (T − Ts)/(Ti − Ts) = erf(x/2√αt); contact Ts weighted by √(kρcp).

Copper ball Bi 0.00075; brass 448 °C; shaft T0 390 °C, 15.9 MJ/m; pipe depth 0.65 m.

Boiling and condensation (A6)

Curve: natural (< 5 °C) → nucleate (5-30, CHF ≈ 1 MW/m2 at C) → transition (30-120) → film (> 120, Leidenfrost at D). Burnout: q > CHF jumps to film boiling at ~1000 °C; design q << CHF.

Drop-wise h 5-10× film-wise, but design for film. Horizontal tube h1 = 0.729[gρl(ρl − ρv)h*fgk3/μΔTD]1/4, N tubes /N1/4, h* = hfg + 0.68cpΔT; vertical 0.943 with L. hhor/hvert = 0.77(L/D)1/4.

33 tubes: 3510 W/m2K, 0.0664 kg/s per m; 10×10: 4875, 3.68 MW, 1.50 kg/s; 15×15: 7150, 0.278 kg/s/m; film boiling 940 W/m.

Convection basics (B1)

Convection = conduction at the wall + fluid motion; h = −k(∂T/∂y)0/ΔT ≈ k/δt, so h falls as δt grows. Velocity layer (ν) vs thermal layer (α); δ/δt ≈ Pr1/3. Turbulent: eddies, thin sublayer, steep gradient, high h.

Re = VL/ν, Pr = ν/α, Nu = hL/k, Gr = gβΔTL3/ν2, Ra = GrPr; Tf = (Ts + T∞)/2. Buckingham: 7 variables − 4 dimensions = 3 groups ⇒ Nu = f(Re, Pr).

Boundary-layer analysis (B2)

Cubic profile ⇒ δ = 4.64x/√Rex (Blasius 5.0); Cf,x = 0.664/√Rex, Cf = 1.328/√ReL. δt = 4.53x/Re1/2Pr1/3 ⇒ Nux = 0.332Rex1/2Pr1/3, average 0.664.

Energy eq: u∂T/∂x + v∂T/∂y = α∂2T/∂y2. Integral: d/dx∫u(T∞ − T)dy = α(∂T/∂y)0. Colburn: StPr2/3 = Cf/2. e−ay profile: h = ka = 96.8. hx = ax−0.1: h̄/h = 1.11.

Flat-plate numericals (B3)

Laminar (Re < 5×105) Nu = 0.664Re0.5Pr1/3; turbulent 0.037Re0.8Pr1/3. Low P: only ρ changes. Unheated start: ×[1 − (ξ/x)3/4]−1/3.

Plastic sheet 437 + 548 = 985 W; 6 kPa air 569 W/m; heated after 12 cm: 262 W/m.

Internal flow (B4)

Re < 2300 laminar, f = 64/Re, Lh = 0.05ReD, Lt = PrLh. Turbulent Nu = 0.023Re0.8Prn (0.4 heating, 0.3 cooling). St = f/8. Fully developed + uniform q: ∂T/∂x = dTm/dx = const. Roughness affects only turbulent f.

Te = Ts − (Ts − Ti)e−hA/ṁcp; Q = hAΔTlm; ΔP = f(L/D)ρV2/2. Annulus h 8200; oil Te 19.71 °C, 67.5 kW, 16.8 kW pump (inlet 20 °C assumed).

Tube banks (B5)

Vmax = STV/(ST − D) (staggered: check SD < (ST + D)/2). In-line Nu = 0.27Re0.63Pr0.36(Pr/Prs)0.25; staggered 0.35(ST/SL)0.2Re0.6...; rows < 16 × F. ΔP = NLfχρVmax2/2.

Geothermal: h 92.2, Te 29.1 °C, 24.9 kW/m, 21 Pa. In-line air: 69.4 °C, 87.7 kW, 0.41 kPa. Water staggered: 8190, 104 rows. Incropera: h 139, 19.8 kW/m.

Natural convection (B6)

β = 1/Tf; vertical 0.59Ra1/4 (L = height); horizontal Lc = A/p, hot up 0.54Ra1/4 (0.15Ra1/3 > 107), hot down 0.27Ra1/4; cylinder Churchill-Chu.

0.6 m plate: vertical 99 W (115 W Churchill-Chu), up 128 W (139 W), down 64 W. 8 cm pipe: 442 W.

Mass transfer (B7)

Fick: JA = −CDABdyA/dx; DAB ∝ T3/2/P. Analogy: T↔C, k↔D, Pr↔Sc, Nu↔Sh. Homogeneous medium: no gradient, no diffusion. Absorption = bulk, adsorption = surface.

Equimolar: NA = CD(y1 − y2)/L. Stagnant gas: NA = (CD/L)ln[(1 − yL)/(1 − y0)]. Sphere: 4πr1r2DΔC/(r2 − r1).

H2 2.48×10−10 kg/s; toluene 5.49×10−7 kg/m2s; beaker 3.48×10−8 kg/s.

★ REMEMBER IT
  • Boiling curve regions in order: natural convection → nucleate (isolated bubbles, then columns) → peak heat flux (critical / burnout point) → transition → film boiling (Leidenfrost). Burnout: past the peak a vapour film blankets the surface, h collapses and the tube temperature jumps to melting.
  • Dropwise condensation gives ~10× higher h than filmwise (no liquid film insulating the surface), but is hard to keep. Horizontal tubes condense better than vertical (thinner film, shorter path), hhoriz/hvert ≈ 0.729/0.943 (L/D)1/4.
Before you start: boiling and condensation in plain words

Boiling is evaporation at a solid-liquid interface when the surface is hotter than the saturation temperature of the liquid (Ts > Tsat): vapour bubbles form on the surface. Condensation is the reverse: vapour touching a surface colder than Tsat turns into liquid. Both involve latent heat, so h is very large (thousands of W/m2K).

Excess temperature ΔTe = Ts − Tsat for boiling, Tsat − Ts for condensation. hfg = latent heat (kJ/kg).

Film-wise vs drop-wise condensation (2019 4a, 2021 4a, 2023 4a, 2022 4b)
Film-wiseDrop-wise
Condensate wets the surface and forms a continuous liquid filmCondensate forms droplets that do not wet the surface and roll off
The film is a thermal resistance: vapour must conduct through itMuch of the surface is bare: vapour touches the metal directly
h about 5-20 kW/m2Kh 5-10 times larger (up to 100+ kW/m2K)
Occurs on clean, wettable surfaces; stable, predictable; used for designNeeds non-wetting coatings (Teflon, gold, oils) that wear off; hard to sustain

Which is more effective / preferable? Drop-wise condensation gives much higher heat transfer coefficients, so it is more effective. But it cannot be maintained for long in practice, so condensers are designed for film condensation (conservative). On a vertical plate the Nusselt film theory gives h = 0.943[gρl(ρl − ρv)h*fgkl3/μl(Tsat − Ts)L]1/4: the film thickens downward (δ ∝ x1/4) and h falls (h ∝ 1/δ). Drop-wise condensation avoids this film resistance entirely.

Film condensation on a vertical plate (2023 4a): vapour condenses at the top, the liquid film flows down under gravity, growing thicker as more vapour condenses on it; flow is laminar near the top and may become wavy/turbulent further down (judged by the film Reynolds number). Heat passes by conduction through the film from the liquid-vapour interface (at Tsat) to the wall (Ts).

Boiling vs evaporation (2019 4a): evaporation occurs at a liquid-vapour (free) interface when the vapour pressure is less than the saturation pressure of the liquid at its temperature, with no bubbles, at any temperature (e.g. a wet road drying). Boiling occurs at a solid-liquid interface when the surface is above Tsat, with bubble formation and very high heat flux.

Why condenser tubes are horizontal (2020 2b): for a single tube hhorizontal/hvertical = 0.729/0.943 × (L/D)1/4 = 0.77(L/D)1/4. For L/D = 100, this is 2.4: the condensate film on a horizontal tube is thin because it drains over a short path (around the circumference, length ~D) instead of along the whole tube length L. Horizontal tubes also make the condenser shell compact and easy to drain.

Pool boiling curve (2019 4b, 2020 3b, 2021 4b, 2023 4b, 2022 4a)
  1. Natural convection boiling (ΔTe < 5 °C): liquid near the surface is slightly superheated; it rises by natural convection and evaporates at the free surface; no bubbles on the heater.
  2. Nucleate boiling (5-30 °C, A-C): bubbles form at nucleation sites (cavities, scratches). A-B: isolated bubbles that collapse in the liquid; B-C: bubbles form jets and columns that rise to the surface. Bubble motion stirs the liquid strongly, so q rises steeply. This is the most desirable regime: high q at small ΔT. Point C is the maximum: critical heat flux (CHF), about 1 MW/m2 for water.
  3. Transition boiling (30-120 °C, C-D): part of the surface is covered by a vapour film (a poor conductor) which forms and collapses unsteadily; q decreases as ΔT increases.
  4. Film boiling (> 120 °C, beyond D): a stable vapour blanket covers the surface; heat passes by conduction and radiation through the vapour. Point D (minimum heat flux) is the Leidenfrost point. q rises again at very high ΔT as radiation grows.

Burnout: in electric heaters and nuclear reactors the heat flux q (not the temperature) is controlled. If q is raised beyond the CHF (point C), the surface cannot transfer it by nucleate boiling, a vapour film forms, and the operating point jumps horizontally to the film-boiling curve at the same q, where ΔTe is about 1000 °C. The surface temperature exceeds the melting point of the material and it burns out. In boiler design the heat flux is therefore kept well below CHF (with a safety margin), so that tubes stay in the nucleate regime: high heat transfer, low wall temperature, and no risk of tube rupture.

Physical mechanism of boiling (2022 4a): a vapour bubble can form only on a surface hotter than Tsat and only at nucleation sites where small gas or vapour pockets exist. A bubble grows by evaporation at its base (microlayer), departs under buoyancy when its size reaches a critical diameter, and the cooler liquid rushes in to fill its place: this cycle of bubble formation, growth, departure and liquid replacement removes heat from the surface at very high rates.

LEARN IT FROM ZERO
Thermal resistance, from zero

Heat flowing through a wall behaves exactly like electric current through a resistor: Q = ΔT / R. Temperature difference is the "voltage", heat rate the "current". Each layer and each surface film has its own resistance, and layers one after another simply add (series).

  • Plane wall: R = L/(kA)
  • Convection film: R = 1/(hA)
  • Cylinder layer: R = ln(r2/r1)/(2πkL)
  • Sphere shell: R = (r2 − r1)/(4πkr1r2)

Once you have Q, any inside temperature comes from Q = ΔT/R across the part you want.

Before you start: thermal resistance: the electrical analogy

For steady one-dimensional conduction, Q = ΔT/R exactly like current I = ΔV/R. Each layer or surface film has a resistance (K/W) and resistances in series add. This turns most wall and pipe problems into one line of arithmetic.

Plane wall R = L/(kA); convection film R = 1/(hA); cylinder layer R = ln(r2/r1)/(2πkL); spherical shell R = (r2 − r1)/(4πk r1r2).

r1 = 2.5 cm, r2 = 2.75 cm, r3 = 2.75 + 3 = 5.75 cm; L = 1 mRadii from diameters and insulation thickness.
Ri = 1/(hi2πr1L) = 1/(60 × 2π × 0.025) = 0.1061 K/WInner convection.

5. Wire with heat generation in a ceramic sleeve (2021 1c)
Before you start: heat generation in a long cylinder

Steady, uniform generation ė in a wire of radius r0: (1/r)d/dr(r dT/dr) + ė/k = 0 gives T(r) = Ts + ė(r02 − r2)/(4k), so Tcentre − Tsurface = ėr02/(4k). All the heat generated must leave through the surface: Q = ėπr02L.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
ė = 50 W/cm3 = 50 × 106 W/m3; r1 = 0.002 m, r2 = 0.002 + 0.005 = 0.007 m1 cm3 = 10−6 m3.

Interface: T1 = Ts + Q ln(r2/r1)/(2πkc) = 45 + 628.3 × ln 3.5/(2π × 1.2)The ceramic has no generation: plain cylindrical resistance.
Tinterface = 45 + 104.4 = 149.4 °C
Tcentre = T1 + ėr12/(4kw) = 149.4 + 5×107 × 4×10−6/60 = 152.7 °CWire rise is only 3.3 °C because the wire conducts well.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
Steady, no generation, constant k: (1/r2) d/dr(r2dT/dr) = 0Spherical form of the conduction equation.
r2dT/dr = C1 ⇒ T(r) = −C1/r + C2Integrate twice.
T(r1) = T1, T(r2) = T2 ⇒ C1 = (T1 − T2)r1r2/(r1 − r2)Apply BCs and subtract.
Q = −k(4πr2)dT/dr = −4πkC1Fourier with sphere area; the same at every r.
Q = 4πk r1r2(T1 − T2)/(r2 − r1) ⇒ Rsphere = (r2 − r1)/(4πk r1r2)

Step (write this)Why / what it means
Q = −kA dt/dx ⇒ Q dx = −A k(t) dtSteady: Q is the same at every x, so separate variables.
∫0LQ dx = −A k0∫t1t2(t + 0.5t2)dt
(i) Q = (Ak0/L)[(t12 − t22)/2 + (t13 − t23)/6]Steady heat flow through the wall.
Simplified Fourier form: Q = kmA(t1 − t2)/L ⇒ km = k0[(t1 + t2)/2 + (t12 + t1t2 + t22)/6]Divide (i) by (t1 − t2) using a2 − b2 and a3 − b3 factorisations.
(ii) Mean temperature tm satisfies k(tm) = km: tm + 0.5tm2 = (t1 + t2)/2 + (t12 + t1t2 + t22)/6

8. Overall heat transfer coefficient (2023 2a)

Definition: U (W/m2K) is the heat transfer rate per unit area per unit overall temperature difference between two fluids separated by a wall: Q = UA(Thot fluid − Tcold fluid). It combines all the resistances in one number.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
Hot fluid → wall: Q = h1A(T∞1 − T1) ⇒ T∞1 − T1 = Q/(h1A)Convection on the hot side.
Through wall: Q = kA(T1 − T2)/L ⇒ T1 − T2 = QL/(kA)Conduction.
Wall → cold fluid: T2 − T∞2 = Q/(h2A)Convection on the cold side.
Add: T∞1 − T∞2 = (Q/A)(1/h1 + L/k + 1/h2)Intermediate temperatures cancel.
Q = UA(T∞1 − T∞2), 1/U = 1/h1 + L/k + 1/h2For several layers add ΣLi/ki; for a tube, UA = 1/Rtotal.

How it is measured: in a test (e.g. a heat exchanger or a wall sample between two fluids), measure the heat rate Q (from ṁcpΔT of one fluid or the electrical heater power), the area A and the two fluid temperatures; then U = Q/(AΔT) (for an exchanger use ΔTlm).

Memory trick: "Q = ΔT / ΣR": wall L/kA, film 1/hA, pipe ln(ro/ri)/2πkL, sphere (ro − ri)/4πkriro. Wire: centre is hotter by ėr2/4k.

★ REMEMBER IT
  • Three modes: conduction q = −kA dT/dx (touching, solids), convection q = hA(Ts − T∞) (moving fluid), radiation q = εσA(Ts4 − Tsur4) (no medium needed).
  • k = how well a material conducts; α = k/ρcp = how fast heat spreads through it (k divided by how much heat it soaks up).
  • Boundary conditions: specified temperature, specified heat flux (insulated = zero flux), convection, radiation, interface.
Before you start: what heat transfer is

Thermodynamics tells us how much energy moves from one state to another. Heat transfer tells us how fast it moves (watts) and what the temperature is at every point. Heat always flows from hot to cold, and the driving force is a temperature difference.

Units: heat rate Q in W; heat flux q = Q/A in W/m2; thermal conductivity k in W/m K; heat transfer coefficient h in W/m2 K.

Modes of heat transfer and their governing equations (2022 1a, 2023 1a)
ConductionConvectionRadiation
Mechanismenergy passed from more energetic to less energetic molecules by collisions/lattice vibration and free electronsconduction combined with bulk motion of a fluid next to a surfaceelectromagnetic waves (photons) emitted by matter because of its temperature
Mediumsolids, and liquids/gases at restmoving liquid or gasnone needed (works in vacuum)
LawFourier: Q = −kA dT/dxNewton: Q = hAs(Ts − T∞)Stefan-Boltzmann: Q = εσAs(Ts4 − Tsurr4)
Key propertyk (W/m K)h (W/m2 K), depends on flowemissivity ε (0-1), σ = 5.67×10−8 W/m2K4
Exampleheat through a wall, a spoon in teafan cooling a CPU, wind on a wallsunlight, heat from a fire

Side note: The minus sign in Fourier’s law is there because heat flows down the temperature gradient: if T falls with x (dT/dx < 0), Q is positive in +x.

Thermal conductivity and thermal diffusivity (2019 1a)
  • Thermal conductivity k: the rate of heat transfer through a unit thickness of material per unit area per unit temperature difference (W/m K). It measures how well a material conducts heat. Copper 401, steel 15-60, brick 0.7, glass wool 0.04, air 0.026 W/m K.
  • Thermal diffusivity α = k/(ρcp) (m2/s): heat conducted divided by heat stored per unit volume. It measures how fast heat spreads through a material during transient heating. Large α (metals) ⇒ the body responds quickly to a temperature change; small α (wood, soil) ⇒ slow response.
Steady vs transient heat transfer (2019 2a)
SteadyTransient (unsteady)
Temperature at any point does not change with time: ∂T/∂t = 0Temperature changes with time: ∂T/∂t ≠ 0
Heat in = heat out; no energy storedPart of the heat is stored (or released): energy content changes
Example: heat loss through a house wall on a day with constant conditionsExample: a hot shaft cooling, an egg boiling, a plate in an oven
General heat conduction equation: Cartesian coordinates (2023 1b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Element dx × dy × dz with heat generation ėgen (W/m3), density ρ, specific heat cChoose a tiny volume and apply energy conservation to it.
(Qx + Qy + Qz) − (Qx+dx + Qy+dy + Qz+dz) + Ėgen = dEelement/dtRate in − rate out + generated = rate of change of stored energy.
Ėgen = ėgen dx dy dz; dE/dt = ρc dx dy dz ∂T/∂tGeneration is per unit volume; storage is mass × c × rate of temperature rise.
Divide by dx dy dz: −(Qx+dx − Qx)/(dy dz dx) − ... + ėgen = ρc ∂T/∂t
dx → 0: (Qx+dx − Qx)/dx → ∂Qx/∂x, with Qx = −k dy dz ∂T/∂xDefinition of a derivative + Fourier’s law.
∂/∂x(k∂T/∂x) + ∂/∂y(k∂T/∂y) + ∂/∂z(k∂T/∂z) + ėgen = ρc ∂T/∂tGeneral (three-dimensional) conduction equation.
Constant k: ∂2T/∂x2 + ∂2T/∂y2 + ∂2T/∂z2 + ėgen/k = (1/α)∂T/∂tDivide by k; α = k/ρc.

Special forms: steady (∂/∂t = 0) ⇒ Poisson equation ∇2T + ė/k = 0; transient with no generation ⇒ diffusion (Fourier) equation ∇2T = (1/α)∂T/∂t; steady with no generation ⇒ Laplace equation ∇2T = 0.

General heat conduction equation: cylindrical coordinates (2019 1b, 2022 1b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Element: dr × r dφ × dz; volume dV = r dφ dr dzCylindrical coordinates (r, φ, z) suit pipes and wires.
Areas normal to each direction: Ar = r dφ dz, Aφ = dr dz, Az = r dφ drThe area facing r grows with r: this is what makes the cylindrical equation different.
Qr = −k Ar ∂T/∂r, Qφ = −k Aφ (1/r)∂T/∂φ, Qz = −k Az ∂T/∂zFourier’s law; distance along φ is r dφ.
Energy balance: −(∂Qr/∂r)dr − (∂Qφ/∂φ)dφ − (∂Qz/∂z)dz + ėgendV = ρc dV ∂T/∂tSame balance as the Cartesian case.
Substitute and divide by dV = r dφ dr dz:
(1/r)∂/∂r(kr∂T/∂r) + (1/r2)∂/∂φ(k∂T/∂φ) + ∂/∂z(k∂T/∂z) + ėgen = ρc ∂T/∂tGeneral conduction equation in cylindrical coordinates.
Steady, one-dimensional, no generation: (1/r) d/dr(r dT/dr) = 0The form used for pipes: gives T = C1ln r + C2.

Spherical (for reference): (1/r2)∂/∂r(kr2∂T/∂r) + (1/r2sin2θ)∂/∂φ(k∂T/∂φ) + (1/r2sinθ)∂/∂θ(k sinθ ∂T/∂θ) + ė = ρc ∂T/∂t.

Boundary conditions (2021 1a)
Boundary condition (BC)Mathematical form at x = 0Example
1. Specified temperatureT(0, t) = T1surface in contact with melting ice or boiling water
2. Specified heat flux−k ∂T(0,t)/∂x = q̇0electric heater on a surface
3. Insulated (adiabatic) / symmetry∂T(0,t)/∂x = 0well-insulated face; centre plane of a symmetric wall
4. Convection−k ∂T(0,t)/∂x = h[T∞ − T(0,t)]wall exposed to air
5. Radiation−k ∂T(0,t)/∂x = εσ[Tsurr4 − T(0,t)4]spacecraft surface
6. InterfaceTA(x0) = TB(x0) and −kA∂TA/∂x = −kB∂TB/∂xtwo layers of a composite wall

A steady one-dimensional problem (second-order equation) needs two boundary conditions; a transient problem also needs an initial condition T(x, 0).

Does heat generation violate the first law? (2021 1b)

No. "Heat generation" means the conversion of another form of energy into thermal energy inside the solid: electrical energy in a resistance wire (I2R), chemical energy in a reaction, nuclear energy in a fuel rod, absorbed radiation. Energy is not created; it changes form. The first law Ein − Eout + Egen = ΔEstored simply counts this conversion as a source term. If the source is counted too (e.g. the electrical work entering the wire), the total energy is conserved exactly.

Thermal contact resistance (2019 3a, 2022 2a)

When two solid surfaces are pressed together, they touch only at the peaks of their surface roughness; the gaps are filled with air (a poor conductor). Heat must squeeze through the few contact spots, so there is a sudden temperature drop ΔT at the interface. Thermal contact resistance Rc = ΔTinterface/(Q/A) (m2K/W); its inverse is the thermal contact conductance hc.

Factors: surface roughness; contact pressure (higher pressure → lower Rc); hardness of the materials; interfacial fluid (air, grease, helium); temperature; material conductivities; flatness. It is reduced by thermal grease or a soft metal foil (indium, aluminium).

Memory trick: Modes: "Fourier touches, Newton flows, Stefan shines". Conduction equation: "change in − change out + generation = storage". Laplace = no source, no time; Poisson = source; Fourier/diffusion = time.

LEARN IT FROM ZERO
Fins, from zero

When convection is weak (small h), you cannot easily raise h, so you raise the area: stick thin metal plates or pins on the surface. Heat conducts along the fin and convects off its sides. But the fin gets cooler towards its tip, so the far end works less hard.

The fin equation d²θ/dx² = m²θ with m = √(hP/kAc) describes this. For a long fin or an insulated tip, Q = √(hPkAc) θb tanh(mL). Efficiency = actual heat / heat if the whole fin were at base temperature = tanh(mL)/(mL). Effectiveness = heat with fin / heat from the same base area without it (should be > 2).

Longer fin: more heat in total (effectiveness up) but the extra length is cooler, so efficiency drops. Beyond mL ≈ 2–3, extra length is wasted.

Interactive graph (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: what a fin does

Q = hAsΔT: if h cannot be increased (air) and ΔT is fixed, the only way to remove more heat is to add surface area. A fin (extended surface) is a thin strip or pin of high-k metal attached to a surface. Examples: motorcycle engine cylinders, car radiators, transformer bodies, CPU heat sinks, air-conditioner coils.

Along the fin the temperature falls from Tb at the base towards T∞, so the far parts are less effective. The fin equation describes this fall.

Heat transfer augmentation (2021 2a) means any technique that increases the heat transfer rate for the same temperature difference: fins, rough or ribbed surfaces, twisted tape inserts, vibration, higher flow velocity. It is needed to make heat exchangers, boilers, condensers and electronics cooling smaller, lighter and cheaper, to keep components below their safe temperature, and to save energy and material.

Derivation: fin equation and heat loss with an insulated tip (2019 2b, 2020 2c)

Side note: Assumptions: steady state, constant k, uniform h, no heat generation, one-dimensional conduction along x (thin fin), negligible radiation, uniform cross-section Ac with perimeter p.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
Element dx: Qx = Qx+dx + dQconv, dQconv = h(p dx)(T − T∞)Energy balance: conduction in = conduction out + convection from the side surface.
Qx+dx − Qx = (dQ/dx)dx, Q = −kAcdT/dx ⇒ kAcd2T/dx2 − hp(T − T∞) = 0Taylor expansion + Fourier.
θ = T − T∞, m2 = hp/(kAc): d2θ/dx2 − m2θ = 0Fin equation (T∞ constant so dθ/dx = dT/dx).
General solution θ = C1emx + C2e−mxLinear, second order, constant coefficients.
BCs: θ(0) = θb; insulated tip dθ/dx|x=L = 0Tip heat loss negligible.
C1 + C2 = θb; C1emL − C2e−mL = 0 ⇒ C1 = θbe−mL/(2cosh mL), C2 = θbemL/(2cosh mL)Solve the two equations.
θ/θb = cosh m(L − x)/cosh mLTemperature distribution.
Qfin = −kAcdθ/dx|x=0 = kAcθbm tanh mLAll the heat that leaves the fin enters at the base.
Qfin = √(hpkAc) θb tanh(mL)Because kAcm = √(hpkAc).

Other tips: infinitely long fin Q = √(hpkAc)θb; convective tip: use the insulated-tip formula with corrected length Lc = L + Ac/p (= L + D/4 for a pin, L + t/2 for a plate).

Fin efficiency and effectiveness (2022 2c, 2023 3a, 2020 2c)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
ηfin = Qfin/Qfin,max, Qfin,max = hAfinθbEfficiency: actual heat / heat if the whole fin were at base temperature (infinite k).
For a cylindrical pin with insulated tip Afin = pL: η = √(hpkAc)θbtanh(mL)/(hpLθb)
√(hpkAc)/(hp) = √(kAc/hp) = 1/mSimplify.
ηfin = tanh(mL)/(mL), m = √(4h/kD) for a pinAlways < 1; → 1 for short or very conductive fins.

Effectiveness εfin = Qfin/(hAbθb): heat with the fin divided by heat that the base area Ab would lose without the fin. A fin is worth adding only if ε > 2. For a long fin ε = √(kp/hAc): high k, thin fins and low h (gases) make fins effective.

"Longer fin: more effective, less efficient" (2023 3a). Qfin ∝ tanh(mL), which keeps increasing with L (towards 1), so the heat removed and hence the effectiveness rise with length. But the efficiency tanh(mL)/mL falls because the added outer part is at a temperature close to T∞ and contributes little: the area grows linearly while the heat grows less than linearly. Beyond mL ≈ 2-3 (tanh = 0.96-0.99), extra length adds weight and cost but almost no heat, so practical fins are designed with mL around 1-1.5.

Numerical 1: steel rod (2020 1b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
m = √(hp/kAc) = √(4h/kD) = √(4 × 64/(50 × 0.02)) = 16 m−1; mL = 16 × 0.25 = 4.0For a circular rod p/Ac = 4/D.
√(hpkAc) = √(64 × π × 0.02 × 50 × π × 0.022/4) = 0.2513 W/K
Q = 0.2513 × (120 − 20) × tanh 4 = 25.1 Wtanh 4 = 0.9993: the rod behaves as an infinitely long fin; including tip convection (Lc = L + D/4) also gives 25.1 W.
Numerical 2: parabolic pin fin with blunt tip (2021 2c)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
m = √(4h/kD) = √(4 × 50/(240 × 0.005)) = 12.91 m−1; mL = 12.91 × 0.02 = 0.258Same m definition as a pin.
From Cengel Table 3-3 (parabolic pin, blunt tip): η = 3I1(4mL/3)/[2mL I0(4mL/3)]I0, I1 = modified Bessel functions (table in Cengel).
4mL/3 = 0.344; I1 = 0.1747, I0 = 1.0298 ⇒ η = 3 × 0.1747/(2 × 0.258 × 1.0298) = 0.985Short, highly conductive fin: almost isothermal.
Afin = (πD4/96L2){{[16(L/D)2 + 1]3/2 − 1}} = 2.106×10−4 m2Surface area of the parabolic pin (L/D = 4).
Q = ηhAfin(Tb − T∞) = 0.985 × 50 × 2.106×10−4 × 175 = 1.82 W per fin
Numerical 3: motor body with longitudinal fins (2023 3b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
θb = 62 − 35 = 27 °CAllowed surface excess temperature.
Bare motor surface: Qbare = hπDLθb = 42 × π × 0.4 × 0.25 × 27 = 356 WFirst check if fins are needed at all.
Each fin (length 0.25 m along the motor, thickness t = 0.018, height H = 0.038): p = 2(0.25 + 0.018) = 0.536 m, Ac = 0.25 × 0.018 = 0.0045 m2, m = √(42 × 0.536/(40 × 0.0045)) = 11.18 m−1Fin cross-section seen by the heat flowing outwards.
Qfin = √(hpkAc)θbtanh(mH) = 2.016 × 27 × tanh(0.425) = 21.8 W (26.2 W with tip convection)Insulated-tip formula.
n fins: Q = n Qfin + h(πD − nt)Lθb = 356 + n(21.8 − 5.1) ≥ 350 WFins replace part of the bare surface.
Result: the bare surface already dissipates 356 W > 350 W, so theoretically no fin is needed (n = 0).With the printed data the requirement is met without fins.

Flag: with the printed numbers the bare motor surface (end faces ignored) already removes 356 W at 62 °C. If the examiner intended a larger heat load or a lower h, the method above gives n directly: n = (Qrequired − 356)/(Qfin − htLθb) = (Qrequired − 356)/16.7. For example, 500 W would need (500 − 356)/16.7 = 8.6 → 9 fins. Write the method fully and state the conclusion.

Memory trick: "m = √(hp/kA), Q = √(hpkA)θ tanh mL, η = tanh mL/mL". Long fin: "effective but not efficient".

Past-paper questions · Pass set

  • 2023 Q2(b) [12] Significance of critical thickness of insulation; derive it for a cylindrical object.
  • 2022 Q2(b) [10] Same question: insulation outer radius below critical, insulation removed; justify mathematically.

  • 2021 Q2(b) [15] Explain the concept of critical thickness of insulation. Derive the critical radius for a small hollow pipe.
  • 2020 Q2(a) [10] Define critical radius of insulation. If the outer radius of insulation is less than critical and the insulation is removed, will heat transfer increase or decrease? Justify.

LEARN IT FROM ZERO
Critical radius of insulation, from zero

Wrapping insulation round a thin pipe does two things at once. It adds conduction resistance (good, less heat loss) but it also makes the outer surface bigger, so there is more area for convection to the air (bad, more heat loss). For a thin wire the second effect wins at first: adding insulation increases heat loss, until the outer radius reaches the critical radius rcr = k/h (cylinder) or 2k/h (sphere). Beyond that, more insulation reduces the loss.

So if the insulation's outer radius is below rcr and you remove it, heat loss goes down. This is used on purpose for electric cables: a little insulation helps them cool.

Interactive graph (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: why insulation can increase heat loss

Wrapping insulation around a pipe adds conduction resistance ln(r2/r1)/(2πkL), which reduces heat loss, but it also enlarges the outer surface, so the convection resistance 1/(h2πr2L) falls, which increases heat loss. For a thin pipe the second effect wins at first.

Definition and significance (2019 3a, 2020 2a, 2022 2a, 2023 2b)

The critical radius of insulation rcr is the outer radius of insulation at which the heat loss from a pipe (or sphere) is maximum. Up to rcr adding insulation increases heat loss; beyond it, more insulation reduces heat loss. The critical thickness is rcr − r1.

  • Thermal insulation of a pipe is effective only if the outer radius exceeds rcr; for steam pipes rcr (a few mm) is far smaller than the pipe, so insulation always helps.
  • Electric wires and cables: plastic insulation thinner than rcr actually increases heat dissipation, so the wire runs cooler and can carry more current.
  • Small-diameter tubes (refrigerant lines, thin probes) must be insulated beyond rcr, or the insulation is counter-productive.
Derivation for a cylinder (2021 2b, 2023 2b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Pipe outer radius r1 at T1; insulation k, outer radius r2; air h, T∞; length LSet-up.
Q = (T1 − T∞)/[ln(r2/r1)/(2πkL) + 1/(h2πr2L)]Insulation and convection resistances in series.
Q is maximum when the denominator Rtot(r2) is minimum: dRtot/dr2 = 0Numerator is fixed.
dRtot/dr2 = 1/(2πkLr2) − 1/(2πhLr22) = 0Differentiate ln r2 and 1/r2.
rcr,cylinder = k/hSecond derivative is positive, so it is a minimum of R (maximum of Q).
Sphere: R = (r2 − r1)/(4πk r1r2) + 1/(4πhr22) ⇒ rcr,sphere = 2k/hSame procedure.

Example: glass wool k = 0.05 W/m K in still air h = 5 W/m2K gives rcr = 1 cm.

Insulation thinner than critical is removed: heat loss rises or falls? (2020 2a, 2022 2b)

Heat transfer decreases. Mathematically: for r1 ≤ r2 < rcr, dRtot/dr2 = (1/2πLr2)(1/k − 1/(hr2)) < 0 because hr2 < k. So Rtot falls as r2 grows from r1 to r2, i.e. Rtot(r2) < Rtot(r1) = 1/(h2πr1L) (bare pipe). Since Q = ΔT/Rtot, the insulated pipe loses more heat than the bare pipe; removing the insulation increases the resistance and the heat loss decreases (for the same pipe surface temperature).

Memory trick: "Cylinder k over h, sphere two k over h". Below rcr insulation acts like a fin; above it, like a blanket.

LEARN IT FROM ZERO
Transient conduction, from zero

Drop a hot metal ball into water. Does its inside stay at one temperature while it cools? Only if heat moves through the ball much more easily than it leaves the surface. The Biot number Bi = hLc/k compares the two (Lc = V/As). If Bi ≤ 0.1 the body is "lumped": one temperature everywhere, and it cools exponentially: (T − T∞)/(Ti − T∞) = e−bt, b = hAs/(ρVcp).

If Bi > 0.1 the centre lags behind the surface and you need the Heisler charts or the one-term series solution, using the Fourier number Fo = αt/L² (dimensionless time).

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: how a body heats up or cools down

When a hot object is put in cold air, heat must travel from its inside to its surface (conduction, resistance L/k) and then from the surface to the air (convection, resistance 1/h). The Biot number Bi = hLc/k compares these two resistances. If Bi < 0.1 the inside resistance is negligible and the whole body has nearly one temperature: a lumped system.

Fourier number Fo = τ = αt/Lc2 is dimensionless time: how far heat has penetrated. Lc = V/As (sphere D/6, long cylinder D/4, plate half-thickness).

Lumped system: definition and check (2022 3a)

A lumped system is a body whose interior temperature remains essentially uniform at all times during a heat transfer process, so T = T(t) only. Valid when Bi = hLc/k ≤ 0.1.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
Lc = V/As = (πD3/6)/(πD2) = D/6 = 0.12/6 = 0.02 mCharacteristic length of a sphere.
Bi = 15 × 0.02/401 = 0.00075 < 0.1 ⇒ lumped analysis is appropriateCopper conducts so well that its inside stays uniform.
Derivation: θ/θi = e−Bi·Fo (2019 3b, 2022 3b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Body: volume V, surface As, density ρ, cp, initially Ti, put in fluid T∞ with hSet-up.
hAs(T∞ − T)dt = ρVcpdTHeat in by convection during dt = increase of stored energy.
θ = T − T∞, dθ = dT: dθ/θ = −(hAs/ρVcp)dtSeparate variables.
ln(θ/θi) = −bt, b = hAs/(ρVcp)Integrate from t = 0 (θi) to t.
bt = hAst/(ρVcp) = (hLc/k)(kt/ρcpLc2) = Bi · FoMultiply and divide by kLc; Lc = V/As, α = k/ρcp.
θ/θi = (T − T∞)/(Ti − T∞) = e−bt = e−Bi·FoExponential approach to the fluid temperature; 1/b is the time constant.

The Heisler charts are graphs of the same formula. Heat transferred: Q/Qmax = 1 − 2θ0J1(λ1)/λ1 (cylinder), Qmax = ρVcp(Ti − T∞).

★ REMEMBER IT
  • Dimensionless numbers: Re = inertia/viscous (laminar or turbulent?), Pr = ν/α (momentum vs heat spreading; δ/δt), Nu = hL/k (how much convection beats pure conduction), Gr = buoyancy/viscous (natural convection's Re), Ra = Gr·Pr, St = Nu/(Re Pr).
  • h falls along a plate because the thermal boundary layer thickens: the same ΔT now spreads over a thicker layer, so the gradient at the wall (and h = −k(∂T/∂y)wall/ΔT) gets smaller.
  • Film temperature Tf = (Ts + T∞)/2: evaluate air properties here.
Before you start: what convection is

Convection is heat transfer between a surface and a moving fluid. Right at the wall the fluid is at rest (no-slip), so heat enters the fluid by conduction; the moving fluid then carries it away (advection) and brings fresh cold fluid to the wall. Faster flow = steeper temperature gradient at the wall = more heat.

Newton’s law of cooling Q = hAs(Ts − T∞). The whole of convection theory is about finding h. Since the wall layer is conducting: h = −kfluid(∂T/∂y)y=0/(Ts − T∞).

Physical mechanism of convection (2022 5a, 2023 5a)
  1. A cold fluid at T∞ flows over a hot surface at Ts.
  2. The fluid layer touching the wall sticks to it (velocity 0) and takes the wall temperature; heat passes into this layer by pure conduction: q = −k(∂T/∂y)y=0.
  3. The heated fluid is swept downstream by the flow (energy carried by bulk motion) and replaced by cooler fluid, so the temperature gradient at the wall stays steep.
  4. Convection is therefore conduction + fluid motion. It is forced if the motion is caused by a fan or pump, natural (free) if it is caused by buoyancy (density differences from heating).
  5. h depends on: fluid properties (k, μ, ρ, cp), velocity, geometry and surface roughness, and the flow type (laminar/turbulent). Typical h: free convection of gases 2-25, forced gases 25-250, forced liquids 50-20,000, boiling/condensation 2500-100,000 W/m2K.
Hydrodynamic and thermal boundary layers (2022 5a, 2019 5a, 2023 5b)
Hydrodynamic (velocity) boundary layerThermal boundary layer
Region near the wall where velocity changes from 0 (wall) to 0.99U∞Region where temperature changes from Ts to Ts + 0.99(T∞ − Ts)
Thickness δ, caused by viscosity (momentum diffusion ν)Thickness δt, caused by heat diffusion α
Gives wall shear stress τs = μ(∂u/∂y)0 and frictionGives wall heat flux qs = −k(∂T/∂y)0 and h
Exists whenever a fluid flows over a surfaceExists only if Ts ≠ T∞

Their relative thickness is set by the Prandtl number: δ/δt ≈ Pr1/3. Gases (Pr ≈ 0.7): δ ≈ δt; oils (Pr >> 1): δt << δ; liquid metals (Pr << 1): δt >> δ.

Developing vs fully developed flow (2019 5a): at a pipe entrance the boundary layers grow from the wall; this is the developing (entrance) region, where the velocity/temperature profile changes with x and h is high. Once the boundary layers meet at the centre the profile stops changing shape with x: fully developed flow, with constant friction factor and constant h. (Hydrodynamic entry length Lh ≈ 0.05ReD laminar, ≈ 10D turbulent.)

Why h decreases as the thermal boundary layer grows (2022 5b, 2023 5b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
h = −k(∂T/∂y)y=0/(Ts − T∞)Definition of h from the wall conduction.
The whole temperature drop Ts − T∞ takes place across δt ⇒ (∂T/∂y)0 ≈ (T∞ − Ts)/δtRough estimate of the wall gradient.
h ≈ k/δtThe film acts like a conducting layer of thickness δt.
Laminar flat plate: δt ∝ x1/2 ⇒ hx ∝ x−1/2As the layer thickens downstream, the gradient at the wall becomes gentler, so h falls. Heat must "conduct" through a thicker insulating fluid layer.
Turbulent boundary layer heat transfer (2019 6b, 2021 5a)

Beyond Rex ≈ 5×105 the laminar boundary layer becomes unstable and turns turbulent. The turbulent layer has three zones: a thin viscous (laminar) sublayer at the wall, a buffer layer, and the turbulent core full of random eddies.

  • Eddies move lumps of fluid across the layer, carrying hot fluid outwards and cold fluid towards the wall. This eddy (turbulent) mixing transports heat far faster than molecular conduction (eddy diffusivity εH >> α).
  • Because the core is so well mixed, almost the whole temperature drop is squeezed into the very thin viscous sublayer, so the wall gradient (∂T/∂y)0 is very steep.
  • Therefore hturbulent is several times hlaminar (and so is wall friction). Example: flat plate, laminar Nu ∝ Re0.5, turbulent Nu ∝ Re0.8.
Dimensionless numbers and their significance (2020 4a, 2019 6a, 2023 6a, 2021 6b, 2020 6b)
NumberDefinitionPhysical meaning
Reynolds ReVLc/ν = ρVLc/μinertia forces / viscous forces; decides laminar or turbulent (plate 5×105, pipe 2300)
Prandtl Prν/α = μcp/kmomentum diffusivity / thermal diffusivity; relative thickness of velocity and thermal boundary layers (gases 0.7, water 1.7-13.7, oils 100-40,000, liquid metals 0.01)
Nusselt NuhLc/kfluidconvection heat transfer / conduction across the same fluid layer; Nu = 1 means pure conduction; dimensionless h
Grashof Grgβ(Ts − T∞)Lc3/ν2buoyancy forces / viscous forces; plays the role of Re in natural convection
Rayleigh RaGr·Prbuoyancy-driven flow strength; decides laminar (< 109) or turbulent natural convection on a vertical plate
Stanton Sth/(ρcpV) = Nu/(RePr)heat transferred / heat capacity of the flow

Grashof vs Reynolds (2020 6b): Re compares inertia to viscous forces in forced flow where the velocity is imposed; Gr compares buoyancy to viscous forces in natural convection where there is no imposed velocity (velocity is created by the temperature difference). If Gr/Re2 << 1 natural convection can be ignored; >> 1 forced convection can be ignored; ≈ 1 mixed convection.

Film temperature (2022 6b): Tf = (Ts + T∞)/2, the arithmetic mean of the surface and free-stream temperatures. Fluid properties vary across the boundary layer, so they are evaluated at Tf as a representative average; this makes constant-property correlations (Nu = CRemPrn) accurate for external flow.

Dimensional analysis: Nu = f(Re, Pr) (2021 6a)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
h = f(ρ, μ, cp, k, V, L): 7 variablesVariables affecting h in forced convection.
Basic dimensions M, L, T, θ (4) ⇒ 7 − 4 = 3 π groups (Buckingham π theorem)Dimensions: h [M T−3θ−1], ρ [ML−3], μ [ML−1T−1], cp [L2T−2θ−1], k [MLT−3θ−1], V [LT−1], L [L].
Repeating variables: ρ, V, L, k (contain M, L, T, θ)They must together contain all four dimensions.
π1 = ρaVbLckdh: θ: −d − 1 = 0 ⇒ d = −1; M: a + d + 1 = 0 ⇒ a = 0; T: −b − 3d − 3 = 0 ⇒ b = 0; L: −3a + b + c + d = 0 ⇒ c = 1 ⇒ π1 = hL/k = NuEquate the exponents of each dimension to zero.
π2 = ρaVbLckdμ ⇒ d = 0, a = −1, b = −1, c = −1 ⇒ π2 = μ/(ρVL) = 1/ReSame method.
π3 = ρaVbLckdcp ⇒ d = −1, a = 1, b = 1, c = 1 ⇒ π3 = ρVcpL/k = RePr
Nu = f(Re, Pr), usually Nu = C RemPrnSince π3/π2−1 = Pr; C, m, n come from experiments.
Methods of finding h (2022 8b)
  1. Dimensional analysis + experiments: gives Nu = CRemPrn; constants from tests. Most correlations used in design come from this.
  2. Exact analytical solution of the boundary-layer equations (e.g. Blasius similarity solution for a flat plate).
  3. Approximate integral method (von Kármán): assume velocity and temperature profiles, satisfy the integral momentum and energy equations.
  4. Analogy between heat and momentum transfer (Reynolds, Colburn): St Pr2/3 = Cf/2, so h is found from measured friction, which is easier to measure.
  5. Numerical method (finite difference/volume, CFD): solve the full equations on a grid by computer for complex geometries.

Memory trick: "Convection = conduction at the wall + carrying away". h ≈ k/δt. Re = inertia/viscous, Pr = ν/α, Nu = hL/k, Gr = buoyancy/viscous, Ra = GrPr.

UNDERSTAND Read this to understand; you do not need to write it

Mass transfer is the twin of heat transfer: concentration difference drives it the way temperature difference drives heat. Fick's law j = −D dC/dx is Fourier's law with D (mass diffusivity) in place of α. Evaporation from a liquid at the bottom of a tube into stagnant air (Stefan tube) is faster than plain diffusion because the air must stay still while vapour flows up, giving a log term.

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: mass transfer in plain words

Mass transfer is the movement of a species (a chemical component) from a region of high concentration to low concentration, exactly like heat moving from high to low temperature. Example: the smell of perfume spreading, sugar dissolving in still tea, water evaporating into dry air.

Concentration can be expressed as mass fraction wA = ρA/ρ, molar concentration CA (kmol/m3), or mole fraction yA = CA/C = PA/P for ideal gases; C = P/(RuT), Ru = 8.314 kJ/kmol K.

Fick’s law and mass diffusivity (2019 8a, 2020 6a, 2021 8b, 2022 8a, 2023 8a)

Fick’s law: the rate of diffusion of a species A per unit area is proportional to its concentration gradient: jA = −ρDABdwA/dx (kg/m2s) or, on a molar basis, JA = −CDABdyA/dx (kmol/m2s); for constant density, JA = −DABdCA/dx. The minus sign shows diffusion goes down the concentration gradient.

Mass diffusivity DAB (m2/s): the diffusion coefficient of A through B; it measures how fast a species spreads. Typical: gases ~10−5, liquids ~10−9, solids 10−10-10−34 m2/s. Effect of T and P for gases: DAB ∝ T3/2/P: it rises with temperature (molecules move faster) and falls with pressure (more collisions, shorter free path). So DAB,2 = DAB,1(P1/P2)(T2/T1)3/2.

Analogy between heat and mass transfer (2020 6a, 2023 7a)
Heat transferMass transfer
Driving force: temperature difference ΔTDriving force: concentration difference ΔC
Fourier: q = −k dT/dxFick: j = −ρDAB dw/dx
Thermal diffusivity αMass diffusivity DAB
Prandtl Pr = ν/α, Nusselt Nu = hL/kSchmidt Sc = ν/DAB, Sherwood Sh = hmL/DAB
Lewis number Le = α/DAB = Sc/Pr links the twoCorrelations swap: Nu = CRemPrn ↔ Sh = CRemScn

Examples (2023 7a): (i) liquid to gas: evaporation of water from a lake or a wet cloth into air, a cooling tower; (ii) solid to gas: sublimation of naphthalene balls (moth balls) or dry ice into air, drying of wood/grain.

Mass transfer vs bulk flow (2020 6c): bulk fluid flow moves the whole fluid, all species together, driven by a pressure difference (a fan or pump); it occurs even in a homogeneous mixture. Mass transfer (diffusion) moves one species relative to the mixture, driven by a concentration difference. Can mass transfer occur in a homogeneous medium? No: a homogeneous medium has the same concentration everywhere, so there is no concentration gradient and no driving force for mass transfer (bulk flow can still occur).

Absorption vs adsorption (2021 8a, 2022 8a, 2023 8a)
AbsorptionAdsorption
Substance enters the whole volume (bulk) of the other phaseSubstance sticks only on the surface of a solid
Bulk phenomenon; uniform throughoutSurface phenomenon; concentration higher at the surface
Rate uniform; continues until the solution is saturatedRate fast at first, then slows as the surface fills
Examples: CO2 absorbed in water (soda), ammonia in water (absorption refrigerator), water in a spongeExamples: activated charcoal removing odour, silica gel drying air, gas masks

Simple distillation (2021 8a): a liquid mixture is heated in a still (flask/boiler); the more volatile component (lower boiling point) vaporises more; the vapour rises into a condenser (cooled by water) where it turns back to liquid and is collected in a receiver as the distillate, richer in the volatile component, while the less volatile component stays in the still. Sketch: heater → boiling flask with thermometer → side-arm → water-cooled condenser → receiver.

Steady equimolar counter-diffusion (2019 8b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Gases A and B in a tube of length L between two reservoirs at the same total P and T; A diffuses one way, B the other waySet-up: total pressure constant.
C = CA + CB = P/(RuT) = constant ⇒ dCA/dx = −dCB/dxTotal concentration fixed.
Net molar flow is zero: NA = −NB (equimolar)Each mole of A going right is replaced by a mole of B going left, so there is no bulk motion.
NA = −CDABdyA/dx (no bulk-flow term)Fick’s law alone.
Integrate from x = 0 (yA,1) to L (yA,2) with NA constant (steady)
NA = CDAB(yA,1 − yA,2)/L = (DAB/RuT)(PA,1 − PA,2)/LMolar flux (kmol/m2s); multiply by the area for the rate; NB = −NA. The concentration profile is linear.
Numerical 1: hydrogen diffusing through a nickel sphere (2021 8c)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
r2 = 4.8/2 = 2.4 m, r1 = 2.4 − 0.06 = 2.34 m; DAB(H2 in Ni, 358 K) = 1.2×10−12 m2/sDiameter as printed (4.8 m); DAB from the figure/data.
Steady diffusion through a spherical shell (like heat conduction): N = 4πr1r2DAB(CA1 − CA2)/(r2 − r1)Same form as Q = 4πkr1r2ΔT/(r2 − r1).
N = 4π × 2.34 × 2.4 × 1.2×10−12 × (0.087 − 0)/0.06 = 1.23×10−10 kmol/s
ṁ = NM = 1.23×10−10 × 2.016 = 2.48×10−10 kg/sMolar mass of H2 = 2.016 kg/kmol.
Diffusion of a vapour through a stagnant gas (Stefan flow)

When a liquid A evaporates into a column of gas B that cannot dissolve in the liquid, B is stagnant (NB = 0) and the bulk motion of the mixture helps A upward: NA = (CDAB/L) ln[(1 − yA,L)/(1 − yA,0)], with yA,0 = Psat/P at the liquid surface.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
C = P/(RuT) = 101.325/(8.314 × 291.85) = 0.04176 kmol/m3
yA,0 = 0.026 atm/1 atm = 0.026; yA,L = 0 (fresh air at the top)
NA = (0.04176 × 0.826×10−5/1.524) ln[(1 − 0)/(1 − 0.026)] = 2.263×10−7 × 0.02634Stefan flow.
NA = 5.96×10−9 kmol/m2s = 5.49×10−7 kg/m2sMolar mass of toluene C7H8 = 92.14 kg/kmol.

Step (write this)Why / what it means

Memory trick: "Fick = Fourier with C for T and D for k". Equimolar: linear, N = CDΔy/L. Stagnant gas: add ln[(1 − yL)/(1 − y0)]. Absorption = sponge (bulk); adsorption = sticker (surface).

Before you start: the integral method in one picture

Instead of solving the boundary-layer equations exactly, we assume a reasonable shape for the velocity (or temperature) profile, e.g. a cubic, and force it to satisfy the integral (whole-layer) balance of momentum or energy. This gives δ(x) or δt(x) and from it the friction coefficient and h.

Cubic profile u/U = (3/2)(y/δ) − (1/2)(y/δ)3 satisfies u(0) = 0, u(δ) = U, ∂u/∂y(δ) = 0, ∂2u/∂y2(0) = 0.

Velocity boundary-layer thickness (2020 4b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Integral momentum equation (zero pressure gradient): d/dx∫0δρu(U − u)dy = τs = μ(∂u/∂y)y=0Momentum lost by the layer = wall shear (von Kármán).
BCs: y = 0: u = 0, ∂2u/∂y2 = 0; y = δ: u = U, ∂u/∂y = 0 ⇒ u/U = (3/2)(y/δ) − (1/2)(y/δ)3Fit u = a + by + cy2 + dy3 to the four conditions: a = 0, c = 0, b = 3U/2δ, d = −U/2δ3.
∫0δu(U − u)dy = (39/280)U2δSubstitute and integrate the polynomial.
τs = μ(3U/2δ)Differentiate the profile at y = 0.
(39/280)ρU2dδ/dx = 3μU/(2δ) ⇒ δdδ = (140/13)(ν/U)dxSubstitute into the momentum equation.
δ2/2 = (140/13)(νx/U) (δ = 0 at x = 0)Integrate.
δ/x = 4.64/√Rex√(280/13) = 4.64. Blasius exact: 5.0/√Rex.
Average friction coefficient (2020 5a)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
τs = 3μU/(2δ) = (3μU/2)(√Rex/4.64x)Wall shear from the profile.
Cf,x = τs/(ρU2/2) = 0.646/√RexLocal friction coefficient (Blasius exact: 0.664).
Cf = (1/L)∫0LCf,xdx = (0.646/L)√(ν/U)∫0Lx−1/2dxAverage over the plate.
Cf = 1.29/√ReL (exact Blasius: 1.328/√ReL)Average = 2 × local value at x = L, because of the x−1/2 shape.
Energy equation of the laminar boundary layer (2023 6c)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Element dx × dy (unit depth) in steady 2-D flow, velocities u, v, temperature TControl volume inside the layer.
Energy carried in by flow (net, x and y): −ρcp[∂(uT)/∂x + ∂(vT)/∂y]dxdyEnthalpy convected through the faces.
Net conduction in: k(∂2T/∂x2 + ∂2T/∂y2)dxdyFourier’s law on each face.
Use continuity ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0: ∂(uT)/∂x + ∂(vT)/∂y = u∂T/∂x + v∂T/∂yRemoves the T(∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y) term.
ρcp(u∂T/∂x + v∂T/∂y) = k(∂2T/∂x2 + ∂2T/∂y2) + μΦΦ = viscous dissipation.
Boundary-layer approximation: ∂2T/∂x2 << ∂2T/∂y2, Φ ≈ (∂u/∂y)2The layer is thin.
u∂T/∂x + v∂T/∂y = α∂2T/∂y2 + (ν/cp)(∂u/∂y)2Dissipation is negligible at low speed: u∂T/∂x + v∂T/∂y = α∂2T/∂y2.
Integral energy equation and thermal layer thickness (2022 6a)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Integrate the energy equation across the thermal layer from y = 0 to H (> δt)Integral form, like the momentum one.
d/dx∫0δtu(T∞ − T)dy = α(∂T/∂y)y=0Energy carried by the layer = heat conducted in at the wall.
Profiles: θ = (T − Ts)/(T∞ − Ts) = (3/2)(y/δt) − (1/2)(y/δt)3, u/U cubic in y/δSame shape as the velocity profile.
Let ζ = δt/δ < 1: integral = U(T∞ − Ts)δ(3/20ζ2 − 3/280ζ4) ≈ (3/20)UΔTδζ2Neglect the small ζ4 term.
(3/20)U d(δζ2)/dx = 3α/(2δζ); with δ from the momentum solutionSubstitute the wall gradient.
ζ3 = (13/14)/Pr (with an unheated start length of 0) ⇒ δt/δ = Pr−1/3/1.026Solve; ζ ≈ Pr−1/3.
δt = 4.53x/(Rex1/2Pr1/3)Combine with δ = 4.64x/√Rex.
Local and average Nu from the given profile (2019 5b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
θ = (3/2)(y/δt) − (1/2)(y/δt)3 ⇒ (∂θ/∂y)0 = 3/(2δt)Differentiate at the wall.
hx = k(∂θ/∂y)0 = 3k/(2δt)h = −k(∂T/∂y)0/(Ts − T∞).
Nux = hxx/k = 1.5x/δt = (1.5/4.53)Rex1/2Pr1/3Insert δt.
Nux = 0.332Rex1/2Pr1/3Local.
h̄ = (1/L)∫0Lhxdx, hx ∝ x−1/2 ⇒ h̄ = 2hx=L
Nū = 0.664ReL1/2Pr1/3Average from 0 to L.
Numerical: h from an exponential temperature profile (2023 5c)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Tf = (160 + 20)/2 = 90 °C: kair = 0.03024 W/m K (Cengel A-15)Fluid property at the film temperature.
T − T∞ = (Ts − T∞)e−ay ⇒ (∂T/∂y)0 = −a(Ts − T∞)Differentiate at y = 0.
qs = −k(∂T/∂y)0 = ka(Ts − T∞) = 0.03024 × 3200 × 140 = 13,550 W/m2Conduction into the fluid at the wall.
h = qs/(Ts − T∞) = ka = 96.8 W/m2K
Rough plate with hx = ax−0.1 (2022 6c)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
h̄x = (1/x)∫0xax−0.1dx = (1/x)(a x0.9/0.9)Average from the leading edge to x.
(i) h̄x/hx = 1/0.9 = 1.11Average is 11% above the local value.
(ii) Both curves fall as x−0.1; h̄x lies 11% above hx everywhere, both infinite at x = 0Sketch two falling curves, the average one higher.
Reynolds-Colburn analogy (2022 7a)

The momentum equation u∂u/∂x + v∂u/∂y = ν∂2u/∂y2 and the energy equation u∂T/∂x + v∂T/∂y = α∂2T/∂y2 have the same form. If Pr = 1 (ν = α) and dP/dx = 0, the dimensionless velocity and temperature profiles are identical, so wall friction and wall heat flux are linked: Reynolds analogy St = Cf/2. Colburn extended it to 0.6 < Pr < 60: St Pr2/3 = Cf,x/2 (jH = j-factor). Application: measure or calculate the friction coefficient (easy) and get h without a heat test; e.g. a flat plate Cf,x = 0.664/√Rex gives Nux = 0.332Rex1/2Pr1/3.

Memory trick: "4.64, 4.53, 0.332, 0.664, 1.328": δ, δt, local Nu, average Nu, average Cf. Average = 2 × local at L (laminar). St Pr2/3 = Cf/2.

Before you start: tube banks

Heat exchangers often have many tubes with a fluid flowing across them. Tubes are arranged in-line (one behind another) or staggered (shifted). ST = transverse pitch (across the flow), SL = longitudinal pitch (along the flow), SD = diagonal pitch = √[SL2 + (ST/2)2].

Recipe: Vmax → ReD = VmaxD/ν → Zukauskas Nu → row correction → h → Te from the exponential law → Q = hAsΔTlm → ΔP = NLfχρVmax2/2.

Staggered1000-2×105Nu = 0.35(ST/SL)0.2Re0.6Pr0.36(Pr/Prs)0.25
Bothfewer than 16 rowsmultiply Nu by the row factor F (Cengel Table 7-3), e.g. in-line 6 rows: 0.945; 15 rows: 0.99

B6 Natural (free) convection Likely · 67%Medium

Past-paper questions · Pass set

  • 2023 Q6(b) [15] Same 0.6 m × 0.6 m plate problem (vertical, hot up, hot down).
  • 2022 Q7(b) [5] Differences between forced and natural convection with examples.

UNDERSTAND Read this to understand; you do not need to write it

Hot air is lighter, so it rises along a hot plate on its own: natural convection. Its strength is measured by the Rayleigh number Ra = gβΔTL3Pr/ν² (β = 1/Tf in kelvin for ideal gases). Then Nu = C Ran, h = Nu k/L, Q = hAΔT. A horizontal plate uses L = A/perimeter.

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: natural convection

A hot surface heats the fluid next to it; the warm fluid is lighter and rises, and cooler fluid takes its place. No fan is needed. The driving force is buoyancy, measured by the Grashof number Gr = gβ(Ts − T∞)Lc3/ν2 and Ra = GrPr. For gases β = 1/Tf (in kelvin).

Recipe: Tf → properties, β → Ra → correct correlation for the geometry → h = Nu k/Lc → Q = hAΔT.

Forced vs natural convection (2022 7b)
Forced convectionNatural (free) convection
Fluid motion created by an external device: fan, pump, windFluid motion created by buoyancy from density differences due to heating
Velocity known; Nu = f(Re, Pr)Velocity unknown (results from ΔT); Nu = f(Gr, Pr) = f(Ra)
Higher h (25-250 W/m2K for gases)Lower h (2-25 W/m2K for gases)
Examples: car radiator with fan, air conditioner coil, cooling a CPU with a fanExamples: room radiator, electric transformer in air, hot tea cooling, hot-water pipe in a room
Numerical 1: hot 0.6 m × 0.6 m plate in three positions (2019 7b, 2023 6b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Tf = (90 + 30)/2 = 60 °C: k = 0.02808, ν = 1.896×10−5, Pr = 0.7202, β = 1/333 K−1; A = 0.36 m2, ΔT = 60 °CAir properties at the film temperature.
(i) Vertical, Lc = 0.6 m: Ra = 9.81(1/333)(60)(0.6)3/(1.896×10−5)2 × 0.7202 = 7.65×108Laminar (< 109).
Nu = 0.59Ra1/4 = 98.1; h = 98.1 × 0.02808/0.6 = 4.59 W/m2K; Q = 4.59 × 0.36 × 60 = 99 WChurchill-Chu (Cengel’s choice) gives Nu = 113 and Q = 115 W; either is accepted if stated.
(ii)/(iii) Horizontal: Lc = A/p = 0.36/2.4 = 0.15 m; Ra = 7.65×108 × (0.15/0.6)3 = 1.195×107Ra ∝ L3.
(ii) Hot surface facing up: Nu = 0.54Ra1/4 = 31.7, h = 5.94 W/m2K, Q = 128 WRa is just above 107; 0.15Ra1/3 gives 139 W (Cengel’s answer).
(iii) Hot surface facing down: Nu = 0.27Ra1/4 = 15.9, h = 2.97 W/m2K, Q = 64 WWarm air is trapped under the plate: the poorest case.

Ranking: hot face up > vertical > hot face down: warm air rises freely from an upward-facing hot plate but must creep around the edges of a downward-facing one.

★ REMEMBER IT
  • Inside tubes: laminar if Re < 2300. Fully developed laminar, constant heat flux: Nu = 4.36; constant wall temperature: Nu = 3.66. Turbulent: Dittus-Boelter Nu = 0.023Re0.8Prn (n = 0.4 heating, 0.3 cooling). Exit temperature: (Ts − Te)/(Ts − Ti) = exp(−hAs/ṁcp).
Before you start: flow inside a pipe

In a pipe the fluid is enclosed, so its temperature changes along the pipe. We use the mean (bulk) temperature Tm, and the energy balance Q = ṁcp(Te − Ti). Laminar if Re = VD/ν < 2300; turbulent above about 10,000.

For constant surface temperature: Te = Ts − (Ts − Ti)exp(−hAs/ṁcp), Q = hAsΔTlm, ΔTlm = (ΔTi − ΔTe)/ln(ΔTi/ΔTe).

Entry lengths for Pr = 0.7 and Pr = 7 (2021 5d)

Laminar: Lh ≈ 0.05ReD, Lt ≈ 0.05RePrD = Pr Lh. For Pr = 0.7 (air) the thermal layer grows slightly faster: Lt = 0.7Lh. For Pr = 7 (water) Lt = 7Lh: the velocity profile becomes fully developed long before the temperature profile.

Axial temperature gradient in fully developed flow with uniform qs (2021 7a, 2023 8c)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Thermally fully developed: ∂/∂x[(Ts − T)/(Ts − Tm)] = 0The shape of the dimensionless profile no longer changes with x.
⇒ (Ts − T)/(Ts − Tm) = f(r) only; differentiating at the wall, h = qs/(Ts − Tm) = constanth does not change with x.
Uniform qs and constant h ⇒ Ts − Tm = qs/h = constant ⇒ dTs/dx = dTm/dxWall and mean temperatures rise in parallel.
Expand: dTs/dx − ∂T/∂x − f(r)(dTs/dx − dTm/dx) = 0Derivative of the product.
∂T/∂x = dTs/dx = dTm/dx = qsp/(ṁcp) = constantThe axial gradient is the same at every r (independent of radial position), from the energy balance ṁcpdTm = qsp dx.
Reynolds analogy for a tube: St = f/8 (2021 5b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Wall shear in a tube: τs = (f/8)ρV2Definition of Darcy friction factor f.
Reynolds analogy (Pr = 1): momentum and heat are carried by the same eddies, so qs/τs = cp(Ts − Tm)/VRatio of heat flux to momentum flux equals the ratio of the driving potentials.
h(Ts − Tm) = (f/8)ρV2cp(Ts − Tm)/VSubstitute qs = hΔT.
St = h/(ρcpV) = f/8Colburn form for Pr ≠ 1: St Pr2/3 = f/8.

Roughness (2021 5c): in turbulent flow roughness elements poke through the thin viscous sublayer, create extra eddies and raise the friction factor (Moody chart, Colebrook equation), so the pressure drop increases (h also rises somewhat). In laminar flow f = 64/Re regardless of roughness: the thick viscous layer covers the roughness, so it has no noticeable effect on the pressure drop.

Numerical 1: water in an annulus (2021 6c)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Dh = Do − Di = 0.050 − 0.035 = 0.015 mHydraulic diameter 4A/p of an annulus.
Tm = (20 + 34)/2 = 27 °C: ν = 0.854×10−6 m2/s, k = 0.610 W/m K, Pr = 5.84Water properties at the mean bulk temperature.
Re = VDh/ν = 2 × 0.015/0.854×10−6 = 35,130 ⇒ turbulent
Nu = 0.023Re0.8Pr0.4 = 0.023 × 35,1300.8 × 5.840.4 = 201.7n = 0.4 because the water is being heated.
h = Nu k/Dh = 201.7 × 0.610/0.015 = 8200 W/m2K
Numerical 2: oil pipeline through an icy lake (2019 6c)

Assumption: the oil inlet temperature is not given in the question; it is taken as 20 °C, as in Cengel Example 8-6 on which the question is based. Properties of oil at 20 °C: ρ = 888.1 kg/m3, k = 0.145 W/m K, ν = 9.429×10−4 m2/s, cp = 1880 J/kg K, Pr = 10,863.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
Re = VD/ν = 2 × 0.3/9.429×10−4 = 636 ⇒ laminar
Lt = 0.05RePrD = 0.05 × 636 × 10,863 × 0.3 = 103,700 m >> 200 mThe whole pipe is a thermal entry region.
Nu = 3.66 + 0.065(D/L)RePr/[1 + 0.04((D/L)RePr)2/3] with (D/L)RePr = 10,360 ⇒ Nu = 37.3Developing laminar flow correlation.
h = 37.3 × 0.145/0.3 = 18.0 W/m2K; As = πDL = 188.5 m2; ṁ = ρ(πD2/4)V = 125.6 kg/s
(i) Te = 0 − (0 − 20)exp(−18.0 × 188.5/(125.6 × 1880)) = 19.71 °COil barely cools: huge mass flow.
ΔTlm = (20 − 19.71)/ln(20/19.71) = 19.86 °C; (ii) Q = hAsΔTlm = 18.0 × 188.5 × 19.86 = 67.5 kW
f = 64/Re = 0.1006; ΔP = f(L/D)ρV2/2 = 0.1006 × (200/0.3) × 888.1 × 22/2 = 119.1 kPa
(iii) Ẇpump = V̇ΔP = (ṁ/ρ)ΔP = 0.1414 × 119.1 = 16.8 kW

Memory trick: "Laminar 64/Re and 0.05Re(Pr)D; turbulent 0.023Re0.8Pr0.4 heat / 0.3 cool". Fully developed + uniform q: everything rises at the same rate dTm/dx.

B3 External forced convection over a flat plate: numericals Possible · 47%Medium

Past-paper questions · Pass set

  • 2022 Q5(c) [12] Air at 5 m/s, 1 atm, 28 °C over a plate at 95 °C heated from x = 12 cm: total heat transfer up to x = 40 cm.
  • 2020 Q5(b) [20] Plastic sheet 1.2 m wide, 2 mm thick, 15 m/min, 90 °C, air 3 m/s at 30 °C on both sides, 2 s in the cooling section, ε = 0.9. Find the heat transfer rate.
  • 2019 Q5(c) [15] Air at 6 kN/m2, 300 °C, 10 m/s over a 0.5 m plate kept at 27 °C: cooling rate per unit width.

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: flat-plate recipe

1) Film temperature Tf = (Ts + T∞)/2 → properties k, ν, Pr. 2) ReL = VL/ν (L in the flow direction). 3) Laminar if ReL < 5×105: Nu = 0.664ReL0.5Pr1/3; turbulent: Nu = 0.037ReL0.8Pr1/3; mixed: (0.037Re0.8 − 871)Pr1/3. 4) h = Nu k/L. 5) Q = hA(Ts − T∞).

Numerical 1: cooling of a plastic sheet (2020 5b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Sheet moves 15 m/min = 0.25 m/s; in 2 s it travels 0.5 m ⇒ cooling section is 0.5 m long and 1.2 m wideFind the length of sheet inside the section.
Air flows across the 1.2 m width: L = 1.2 m; area of both sides A = 2 × 1.2 × 0.5 = 1.2 m2Flow direction is along the width (Cengel Problem 7-23).
Tf = (90 + 30)/2 = 60 °C: k = 0.02808, ν = 1.896×10−5, Pr = 0.7202Air properties at 1 atm.
ReL = 3 × 1.2/1.896×10−5 = 1.90×105 < 5×105 ⇒ laminar
Nu = 0.664(1.90×105)0.5(0.7202)1/3 = 259.3; h = 259.3 × 0.02808/1.2 = 6.07 W/m2K
Qconv = 6.07 × 1.2 × (90 − 30) = 437 W
Qrad = εσA(Ts4 − Tsurr4) = 0.9 × 5.67×10−8 × 1.2 × (3634 − 3034) = 548 WSurroundings taken at the air temperature 30 °C.
Qtotal = 437 + 548 = 985 WRadiation is larger than convection at such low h.

At 163.5 °C: μ = 2.457×10−5, k = 0.03587, Pr = 0.698; ρ = P/RT = 6000/(287 × 436.65) = 0.0479 kg/m3μ, k, Pr are nearly independent of pressure; ρ ∝ P.
ν = μ/ρ = 5.13×10−4 m2/s (about 17 times the 1 atm value)

Nu = 0.664 × 97400.5 × 0.6981/3 = 58.1; h = 58.1 × 0.03587/0.5 = 4.17 W/m2K

Side note: Interpretation: the plate is at the air temperature for 0 ≤ x < ξ = 0.12 m and at 95 °C from x = 0.12 m to 0.40 m; result per metre width.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
Tf = (95 + 28)/2 = 61.5 °C: k = 0.02891, ν = 1.912×10−5, Pr = 0.703
ReL = 5 × 0.40/1.912×10−5 = 1.046×105 ⇒ laminar

Memory trick: "Film, Re, check 5×105, 0.664, h, Q". Low pressure: only ρ (so ν) changes. Starting length: ×[1 − (ξ/x)3/4]−1/3.
